server.bindAddressHint: Bind address: local IP to listen on. Empty = all interfaces.
server.allowedSourcesHint: Allowed sources: IPs or CIDR ranges, comma-separated. Empty = allow all. Note: UDP sources can be spoofed.
server.maxConnsPerIPHint: Maximum concurrent TCP/TLS connections from a single source IP. Raise it for a syslog relay or NAT gateway that multiplexes many senders behind one address.

filter.sourceIPHint: An address (10.0.0.5), a CIDR range (10.0.0.0/24), a pattern (10.0.0.*), or part of an address
filter.modeText: Text: these words in this order, the last one possibly unfinished (click for FTS)
filter.modeFts: FTS: words with AND or a space, OR, NOT, (parentheses), "phrase", prefix* (click for Regex)
filter.modeRegex: Regex search (click to switch to Text)

searchError.unexpectedParen: a closing parenthesis has no opening one
searchError.missingTerm: nothing to search on one side of {term}
searchError.notNeedsLeft: NOT excludes from what comes before it, as in error NOT timeout
searchError.noWords: {term} has no letter or digit to search for
searchError.nearDistance: NEAR takes a distance in words after a comma, as in NEAR(error timeout, 5)
searchError.nearWordsOnly: NEAR takes only words, as in NEAR(error timeout, 5)

filter.exportingDisplayed: Anonymous mode: exporting the values shown on screen.

import.title: Import a log file
import.intro: Read a log file that is already on disk. A captured syslog file is parsed exactly as it would be off the wire; for a plain application log the timestamp and the level are read out of the text, and you see what was recognised before anything is imported.
import.shape_bsd: Syslog without a priority, as written to a file
import.shape_plain: Plain text with a timestamp or a level
import.inferred: Out of {total} plain lines, a timestamp was recognised on {time} and a level on {level}. The rest keep the default.
import.persistHint: Off by default: imported lines would then appear in History next to received traffic.
import.noAlertsHint: An import is history, not traffic: it never fires alert rules and is never relayed to a notification destination.
import.hint_auto: Reads a timestamp at the front of the line and a severity word standing on its own. Right for most files, and it says how much it recognised.
import.hint_syslog: Every line through the syslog parser. A line without a priority belongs to the one above it.
import.hint_json: One JSON object per line. The usual field names are tried, including numeric levels and epoch timestamps.
import.hint_access: The Common and Combined formats. The timestamp is the one in brackets, and the status code is the severity: 5xx an error, 4xx a warning.
import.hint_logfmt: Lines of key=value pairs. Pairs that are not fields are kept in the message.
import.hint_custom: A regular expression run against each line.
import.hint_bsd: A timestamp, a host and a tag, with no priority — what syslog daemons write to a file. A line without that shape belongs to the one above it.
import.hint_apache: Apache's error log: a bracketed header with the year last, the level in [module:level], and the pid in its own bracket.
import.hint_klog: Kubernetes components. The severity is the leading letter, the date carries no year, and the source file stands where an application name would.
import.hint_logcat: Android, in either form: the threadtime lines adb writes to a file, and the brief “E/Tag( 1234):” lines it prints.
import.hint_epoch: A Unix timestamp to the millisecond at the front of the line and nothing else a reader would recognise as a date, as Squid and several proxies write.
import.hint_clef: Serilog's compact event format, where the fields are @t, @l and @m.
import.fieldsHint: Leave a box empty to try the usual names.
import.patternHint: The groups read are time, level, host, app and msg. For example: ^(?P<time>\S+) (?P<level>\w+) (?P<msg>.*)$
import.timeLayoutHint: A Go reference layout, for a timestamp the known shapes do not cover. Empty tries them all. For example 02/01/2006 15:04:05 for a day-first date.
import.joinHint: A line that does not start a record is added to the one above it, so a stack trace is one message at the right severity instead of twenty.
import.skip: Skip lines that do not match
import.skipHint: Off by default: dropping log lines without being asked is the one thing an importer must not do.

log.emptyState: No syslog messages received yet. Start the server and send syslog data.
log.resizeHint: Drag to resize, double-click to fit the widest value
log.moveHint: Click to sort, drag to move the column
log.createAlert: Create an alert rule from this line
log.resizePanel: Drag to resize, double-click to reset
log.freezeHint: Hold the list still while you read it
log.macRouted: Not on this computer’s networks — a MAC is only known on the local network
log.macUnknown: Not in the neighbor table yet

tls.title: TLS Configuration
tls.caDesc: Self-signed root CA. The CA certificate will be uploaded to the device.
tls.caGenerated: CA certificate generated. Now generate the server certificate (Step 2).
tls.serverCertDesc: Signed by the CA above. The SAN IP address must match the server's IP used by the device.
tls.sanWarning: The device (socat verify=1) verifies the server certificate SAN against the connection IP. Make sure the IP address above matches!
tls.serverCertGenerated: Server certificate generated and signed by CA. Ready to start TLS server.
tls.tlsReady: TLS ready. Enable TLS in server controls and click Start.
tls.tlsReadySub: Upload the exported CA certificate (ca-cert.pem) to the device's security page.
tls.loadExistingCertDesc: Use pre-existing PEM certificate and key files for the TLS server.
tls.subject: Subject

settings.title: Settings
settings.clearConfirm: This will permanently delete all stored logs. Continue?
settings.timezoneHint: Applies to every timestamp shown and exported. Stored data is unchanged.

alerts.patternPlaceholder: Text or regex to match in message
alerts.noRules: No alert rules configured. Click "Add Rule" to create one.

encryption.title: Encryption
encryption.hint: When enabled, the database is encrypted when the app closes and decrypted on startup with your password.
encryption.serviceSeal: This window drives the service, which stores its messages unencrypted. Encrypting makes the service seal what it receives for this window and keep no database: its messages move into this window’s database, encrypted, whenever the window is open and unlocked. It takes one administrator prompt.
encryption.serviceSealOwnEncrypted: This window’s own database is encrypted already: type its password.
encryption.serviceSealed: The service now seals what it receives. Its messages are moving into your encrypted database.
encryption.lockedOut: Too many failed attempts. The application will close.
encryption.enableSuccess: Encryption enabled. The database will be encrypted when the app closes.
encryption.unlockMessage: The log database is encrypted. Enter your password to unlock.
encryption.leftClear: This database was found unencrypted: SyslogStudio had decrypted it and then stopped without closing — a crash, a forced stop, a power cut. Type your password: it is checked, the database opens as it was, and it is encrypted again when SyslogStudio closes.
encryption.warningMessage: The encryption password is never stored on disk. It exists only in memory while the app is running.
encryption.warningPoint1: If you forget your password, your log database will be permanently inaccessible.
encryption.warningPoint2: Without the password or a recovery key, nothing can be recovered: the data is encrypted with AES-256. Create a recovery key once encryption is on.
encryption.warningPoint3: Make sure to remember your password or store it in a password manager.
encryption.lockedOutSeconds: Too many failed attempts. Locked for {seconds}s.

warnings.caKeyUnencrypted: Warning: the certificate authority private key is stored unencrypted on disk.

simulator.contentHint: Overrides apply to every message. A custom message is sent verbatim, which is what you want to reproduce one parser input or trip one alert rule.
simulator.customPlaceholder: Leave empty to generate realistic messages
simulator.modeHint_alertTest: Sends a fixed set of messages shaped to match typical alert rules, so rules can be verified on demand.
simulator.modeHint_burst: Sends a fixed number of messages as fast as the transport allows.
simulator.modeHint_continuous: Sends at a steady rate until stopped, or until the duration elapses.
simulator.modeHint_scenario: Walks an incident timeline: quiet, rising load, crisis, then recovery. The profile follows each phase.
simulator.skipVerifyHint: Accept any server certificate. Needed for a collector using a self-signed certificate.
simulator.subtitle: Generate traffic and send it to one or more collectors.
simulator.title: Syslog simulator

anonymous.banner: Hostnames, addresses, user names and domains on screen are stand-ins, not the values received. Stored data is unchanged.
anonymous.hint: Replaces hostnames, addresses, usernames, domains and e-mail addresses with stable stand-ins, so a screenshot can be shared. Display only — stored data is unchanged, and an export from here follows what is shown unless you ask for the real values.

notify.authNoneHint: No credential is sent. Usual for a relay that accepts mail from this network without authenticating it.
notify.blockedHint: Messages not sent because their destination was cut off by the rate limiter.
notify.credentialsInClear: Destination credentials are stored unencrypted. Enable at-rest encryption in Settings to protect them.
notify.destinationsFirst: Add a destination first — a rule needs somewhere to send.
notify.loopedHint: Messages not forwarded because they had already been relayed, or because a destination points back at this application. They were still received and stored — only the forward was stopped. Check your destination addresses.
notify.maxRateHint: Averaged over 30 seconds. A destination that goes far past this, or that floods with repeating content, is cut off automatically and disabled. Leave at 0 for the default, or set a negative value to remove the limit.
notify.mtlsHint: The CA verifies the far end and may be a different authority from the one this app serves its own listener with. A client certificate and key together enable mutual TLS.
notify.name: Name
notify.noDestinations: No destination yet. Add one to start routing.
notify.noRoutes: No rule yet. A destination only receives what a rule sends it.
notify.routeHint: Rules are evaluated by priority, lowest first. An empty field is no constraint, so a rule with none matches everything.
notify.securityMtls: Mutual TLS — also present a client certificate
notify.securityMtlsHint: The server's certificate is verified and this client presents one of its own. The CA may be a different authority from the one signing the client certificate.
notify.securityTlsHint: The server's certificate is verified. Leave the CA empty to use the system trust store, or point it at your own authority.
notify.subtitle: Send matching messages on to another collector, a webhook, or e-mail.
notify.templateHint: Templates accept {{.Hostname}}, {{.Severity}}, {{.Message}}, {{.AppName}}, {{.SourceIP}}, {{.Timestamp}} and the other message fields.
notify.title: Routing and notifications
notify.trippedHint: This destination was cut off automatically. See the delivery log for why, then re-enable it once the cause is fixed.

close.backgroundHint: The window hides. Messages keep arriving, history keeps filling and routing keeps delivering. Open it again from the tray icon.
close.backgroundNoTrayHint: The window hides and everything keeps running. No system tray was found, so start SyslogStudio again to bring the window back.
close.question: What should closing the window do?
close.questionRunning: The receiver is running. What should closing the window do?
close.quitHint: Stops listening. Nothing is received while the application is closed.
close.rememberHint: You can change it later in Settings.
close.title: Close SyslogStudio

background.intro: SyslogStudio can keep receiving without this window, in two different ways.
background.userText: This application starts when you sign in, hidden in the tray, under your account and with your settings. It stops when you sign out. No administrator rights needed.
background.launchAtLogin: Start SyslogStudio when I sign in
background.launchAtLoginHint: It starts hidden in the system tray.
background.registeredElsewhere: Another copy is registered: {path}. Turning this on replaces it with this one.
background.launchUnsupported: Starting at sign-in is not available on this system.
background.autoStartHint: With the listeners as last saved. If the database is encrypted, receiving starts once you have typed the password.
background.autoStartDriving: Does not apply while this window drives the service: the service does the receiving, and its own setting is below.
background.listenOnStart: Start receiving when the service starts
background.listenOnStartHint: With the listeners as last saved. Turned off, the service still starts with the computer, but receives nothing until you press Start in this window.
background.noTray: No system tray was found: a hidden start shows the window minimised instead.
background.serviceText: A separate copy that Windows starts with the computer, before anyone signs in, under its own account (NT SERVICE\SyslogStudio). It keeps its own configuration and database in {dir}, readable by administrators only.
background.serviceUnsupported: The system service is available on Windows and on Linux with systemd. Here, run SyslogStudio --headless under the platform's service manager (launchd on macOS).
background.mustBePerMachine: To run as a service, SyslogStudio must be installed for all users, in Program Files. The service runs under a system account, and a copy that an ordinary user can replace would hand that account to whoever replaces it.
background.otherCopy: The installed service runs another copy: {path}. Updating its configuration points it at this one.
background.viewerDriving: This window drives the service: the settings, messages and rules it shows are the service's, and what you change applies to it.
background.viewerLocal: While the service runs, this window drives it: its settings, its messages, its rules. Until then, it shows your own receiver.
background.updateHint: Copies this window's current settings to the service and restarts it.
background.installTitle: Install SyslogStudio as a system service
background.installStep1: Windows asks for administrator rights, once.
background.installStep2: The service is created and will start with the computer, under NT SERVICE\SyslogStudio.
background.installStep3: Your listeners, alert rules, routes and destinations — credentials included — and your TLS certificate are copied to it.
background.installStep4: An inbound firewall rule lets it receive on domain and private networks.
background.installStep5: This window stops receiving, and no longer starts receiving on launch: the service takes over the ports.
background.installStep6: This window then drives the service: you change its settings and see its messages from here.
background.installNotCopied: Not copied: the messages already stored here.
background.installBringHistory: Bring the messages stored here to the service
background.installBringHistoryHint: Copied in the background once the service runs, and kept here too. The History shows them as they arrive.
background.installNotCopiedEncrypted: Not copied: your encrypted messages stay in this window’s database, which the History no longer shows while the window drives the service. Removing the service later brings its messages back into it.
background.installHistorySealed: Your history stays in your encrypted database here, and what the service receives joins it.
background.installPlaintext: The service stores its messages unencrypted in {dir}, readable by administrators only. Its credentials and private key are protected by Windows (DPAPI).
background.installAccept: I understand that the service's database is not encrypted
background.serviceTextLinux: A separate copy that systemd starts with the computer, before anyone signs in, as the syslogstudio system account. It keeps its own configuration and database in {dir}, readable by root only.
background.mustBePerMachineLinux: To run as a service, SyslogStudio must be installed from its package, or copied under /usr/local as root. The service runs under a system account, and a copy that an ordinary user can replace would hand that account to whoever replaces it.
background.installStep1Linux: Your system asks for an administrator's password, once (polkit).
background.installStep2Linux: A syslogstudio system account and a systemd unit are created; the service starts with the computer and may listen on ports below 1024.
background.installStep4Linux: No firewall rule is added: if a firewall filters what comes in, open the ports in it.
background.installPlaintextLinux: The service stores its messages unencrypted in {dir}, readable by root and the service only, credentials and private key included.
background.installSealed: Keep it encrypted: the service seals what it receives
background.installSealedHint: The service stores nothing it can read back. What it receives reaches your encrypted history here once the database is unlocked; meanwhile the live view shows it, and up to 1 GB waits on the service.
background.installClear: Let the service store its messages unencrypted
background.inboxSealed: Sealed inbox: {batches} batches waiting ({size} of {quota} MB).
background.inboxLeft: {batches} sealed batches still wait on the service ({size} MB).
background.inboxDropped: {count} messages could not be kept since the service started: {error}
background.inboxFilling: The sealed inbox is filling up: unlock your database in this window so the messages are collected.
background.bannerDrivingSealedNote: Settings, rules and live messages are the service's; the history is your encrypted database, which collects what the service seals.
background.bannerCollect: The service's sealed messages cannot all be collected:
background.installed: The service is installed and running.
background.updated: The service's configuration has been updated.
background.uninstallText: The service is stopped and removed, along with its firewall rule.
background.uninstallPurge: Also delete its data, including the messages it stored
background.uninstallBringBack: Bring the service’s messages into this window’s database first
background.uninstallBringBackHint: The service stops receiving while they are copied, so that none is lost on the way. Those this window’s database holds already are not doubled.
background.uninstallSealedCollect: What the service still holds sealed is collected into your database first.
background.uninstallNotDriving: This window is not connected to the service, so its messages cannot be brought back: start the service first, or allow your account.
background.uninstallPurgeLoses: The service’s messages will be deleted with its data.
background.copyToService: Bringing your history to the service: {percent} %
background.copyToServiceNote: The History fills up as it goes; the copy here is kept.
background.copyStopped: Bringing your history to the service stopped; it carries on the next time this window drives the service:
background.copiedToService: Your history is on the service: {count} messages brought over.
background.allowed: Your account can now drive the service.
background.bannerDriving: This window drives the SyslogStudio system service{ports}.
background.bannerDrivingNote: Settings, messages and rules are the service's.
background.bannerStopped: The SyslogStudio system service is stopped: this window shows your own receiver.
background.bannerDenied: The SyslogStudio system service is running, but your account is not allowed to drive it.
background.bannerVersion: The system service runs another version of SyslogStudio ({version}): run the installer to update both.
background.bannerNotService: Another program holds the SyslogStudio service's channel: this window will not connect to it.
background.bannerUnreachable: The SyslogStudio system service is not answering: this window shows your own receiver meanwhile.
background.autoStartFailed: Receiving could not start on launch: {error}
background.conflictTitle: Another SyslogStudio is using this data
background.conflictText: A SyslogStudio started with --headless already has this configuration and database open. Two at once would damage the database, so this window will not receive. Stop the other one, then reopen SyslogStudio.

sources.devicesIntro: Every address messages arrive from: heard since SyslogStudio started — or the service, when this window drives it — and kept in the history. A device whose messages bend the RFCs or come without a hostname, and that no rule reads, is marked: it could use one.
sources.devicesAttention: Only those that could use a rule
sources.devicesSummary: {devices, plural, one {# address} other {# addresses}} · {attention, plural, =0 {none could use a rule} one {# could use a rule} other {# could use a rule}}
sources.badgeHostsHint: Several hostnames from one address: a relay, or a device that sends none and has the first word of each message taken for one.
sources.intro: Some devices bend the syslog standard: no hostname, a format of their own, the same priority on everything, a clock in another zone, an encoding other than UTF-8. A rule says how the messages of such a device are read as they arrive, before the live view, the history, the alert rules and the routing see them. The raw message is always kept.
sources.empty: No rule yet. The quickest way to write one is from a message: right-click it, then “Read this device’s messages differently…”.
sources.order: Rules are tried in this order; the first that matches applies.
sources.saved: Rule saved: it applies to the messages that arrive from now on.
sources.lead: How the messages this rule matches are read as they arrive. Every change is tried on the device’s latest messages below; the rule applies to what arrives once it is saved.
sources.name: Name
sources.sourcesHint: Each address is matched whole: one address (10.0.0.9), a CIDR range (10.0.1.0/24), or a pattern where * stands for any characters and ? for one (10.0.2.*).
sources.patternHint: A regular expression, case-insensitive. It tells devices apart behind a relay, where they all arrive from the same address. Every condition given has to match.
sources.howHint: The format reads what follows the priority when the header is not standard, and the message text when it is. Automatic detection keeps the reading as received; the time zone then applies to timestamps that carry none.
sources.levelAuto: Automatic: the priority, unless a field declares one
sources.arrival: Use the arrival time (the device’s clock is wrong)
sources.previewCount: {matched} of the {total} latest messages match this rule. A struck-through value is the one read without it.
sources.previewNone: None of these messages matches the rule yet: check the addresses and conditions.
sources.noSamples: No recent message to try the rule on: it applies to what arrives once saved.
sources.rereadIntro: Rules apply to messages as they arrive. The stored ones can be read again from their raw text, with the rules as they are now — and as this version reads them, for those an older one stored. Imported lines keep their file's reading, and alerts and routing are not run again. Reading again after a rule has changed or gone undoes what it did.
sources.rereadRunning: {read} of {total} messages gone through · {changed} read differently
sources.rereadDone: Done: {read} messages gone through, {changed} read differently.
sources.rereadStopped: Stopped after {read} messages: the {changed} read differently stay so.

no-hostname.name: Sends no hostname
no-hostname.hint: Routers, switches and appliances that leave the hostname out: the word after the timestamp stays in the message, and the hostname is the address it came from.

camera.name: Camera or IoT device
camera.hint: No hostname, and the same priority on everything: the hostname is the address it came from, and the level the word for it in the text.

level-in-text.name: Level in the text
level-in-text.hint: The same priority on every message: the level is the word for it in the text — ERROR, warning, crit…

json.name: JSON behind a syslog header
json.hint: A container or an application logging JSON through syslog (Docker, Kubernetes): the level, time, host and message are read from the JSON.

windows-1252.name: Garbled accents (Windows-1252)
windows-1252.hint: A Windows or older device that does not send UTF-8: its text is decoded as Windows-1252.

bad-clock.name: Clock not to be trusted
bad-clock.hint: A device whose clock nobody set: its messages take the time they arrived.

own-format.name: A format of its own
own-format.hint: A regular expression with named groups — time, level, host, app, msg — to adapt to the lines of the device.

sources.myTemplatesHint: Ways of reading saved under a name of your own, offered when a rule is written and in a file import. They stay in this window’s settings, whichever engine it drives, and travel in exported files.
sources.myTemplatesEmpty: None yet: in a rule’s editor, or in a file import’s format, “Save as a template…” keeps the way of reading.
sources.imported: {rules} rules imported, turned off — check their addresses, then turn them on. {templates} templates added.
sources.hostNone: It sends none: the address it came from
sources.macLocalOnly: MAC addresses come from this computer’s neighbor table (ARP, NDP): only the devices on its own local networks have one. A device behind a router reaches it with the router’s MAC, so none is shown for it.
sources.macRoutedHint: Not on this computer’s networks: its messages arrive through a router, whose MAC is all the table knows.
sources.macUnknown: MAC not in the table yet
sources.macPrivateHint: A locally administered MAC, chosen by the device (a phone’s private address, a virtual machine): it has no maker to name, and may change.
sources.badgeMacChangedHint: This address had another MAC before: {macs}. A device replaced — or two devices claiming one address.
sources.badgeAlsoAtHint: The same MAC was heard from these addresses: the device’s address changed (DHCP).
sources.badgeRuleOldHint: A rule names the address this device had before, and no rule reads it at its new one.
sources.suggestTemplate: Made by {vendor}: the “{template}” template may fit.

storage.alignHint: The limit moves back to the start of its day, week or month, so the oldest period kept is always complete.
storage.continuousHint: Old messages go every few minutes, a little at a time, without holding up those arriving.
storage.scheduleHint: On the machine's clock; run at the next start if SyslogStudio was off. Size and message limits still apply at all times: they protect the disk.
storage.compactAuto: Give it back as it goes (recommended)
storage.compactAutoHint: The space of deleted messages returns to the disk a little at a time, while messages keep arriving.
storage.compactAfterHint: Rewrites the whole database after each scheduled cleanup; messages arriving meanwhile wait in memory, up to 200,000 of them.
storage.compactManualHint: The space is reused for new messages, but the file does not shrink until you press Compact.
storage.compacting: Compacting… messages arriving meanwhile wait in memory.
storage.noData: Not enough messages yet for a forecast.
storage.rate: About {messages} messages a day, {size} a day.
storage.steadyAge: Keeping {days} days holds the database at about {size}
storage.steadyCount: The {count}-message limit holds the database at about {size}
storage.steadySize: The size limit holds the database at {size}
storage.fileStays: The file stays at {size} until compacted.
storage.unbounded: Nothing limits the database: it grows by {size} a day for as long as messages arrive.
storage.diskFull: At this rate the disk ({free} free) is full in about {days} days. Set a retention or a size limit.
storage.lastCleanup: Last cleanup: {when}, {deleted} deleted, {freed} back to the disk
storage.nextContinuous: Next cleanup: within 5 minutes, and every 5 minutes

backup.intro: Copies of the database, encrypted as the database is, sent to every destination below: another disk, a NAS, a server. Each one opens on its own, on another computer if need be.
backup.lockBoth: Backups open with the password or with the recovery key.
backup.lockPassword: Backups open with the password the database had when they were made. A recovery key would open them without it.
backup.lockKey: The database is not encrypted, but its backups are: they open with the recovery key.
backup.lockNone: Backups are not encrypted. Turn on encryption, or create a recovery key, to protect them.
backup.importHint: Add this backup’s messages to the history
backup.importFileHint: Add the messages of a backup, or of a database file (.db), to the history
backup.importTitle: Import a backup into the history
backup.importNote: The messages this backup holds and the history lacks are added to it. Nothing in the history is changed or removed.
backup.importRetention: Messages older than {days} days are removed again at the next cleanup. Lengthen the retention first to keep them.
backup.imported: {added} messages added to the history ({known} were there already).
backup.passwordHint: The password the database had when this backup was made.
backup.restoreWarning: The database will be replaced by this backup. It is copied first, on this computer, so that restoring that copy undoes this. Messages received meanwhile are kept.
backup.restoreRetention: Messages older than {days} days in this backup will be removed at the next cleanup. To read them, open the backup instead, or lengthen the retention first.
backup.opened: The History now shows the backup.
backup.restored: Backup restored. A copy of the previous database is in the list of backups.
backup.viewing: Reading a backup made {when}: {count} messages. The History shows this backup, not the database.
backup.safetyGroup: Before a restore — on this computer

dest.title: Destinations
dest.none: No destination yet: add a folder or a server.
dest.name: Name
dest.folderHint: Another disk, a USB drive, or a network share or NFS export mounted on this machine. With the system service, its account must be able to write there.
dest.keyKept: The key on file is kept
dest.ftpWarningTitle: FTP sends the password in the clear
dest.ftpWarning: Anyone on the network between this computer and the server can read the password, sign in to the server with it, and delete or replace what is there. The backups themselves stay encrypted, but prefer SFTP or FTPS, which most NAS offer.
dest.ftpAck: I understand: the password travels unencrypted
dest.unknown: {host} presents this fingerprint. Compare it with the one its administrator gives you, or the one the NAS shows, and trust it only if they match.
dest.changed: {host} no longer presents the identity it was trusted with. If it was reinstalled or its certificate renewed, trust the new one; otherwise someone may be intercepting the connection.
dest.deleteConfirm: Remove the destination “{name}”? The backups already there stay where they are.

recovery.title: Recovery key
recovery.hint: A file that opens the database and its backups without the password: if the password is forgotten, it gets everything back. Keep it away from this computer — a USB stick, a safe, a password manager.
recovery.created: Recovery key saved. Keep the file somewhere safe: whoever has it can open the database.
recovery.removeConfirm: Remove the recovery key? The file will no longer open the database or new backups; backups made until now still open with it.
recovery.replaceConfirm: Replace the recovery key? The current file will no longer open the database or new backups; backups made until now still open with it.
recovery.useKey: Forgot the password? Use the recovery key
recovery.resetMessage: The recovery key opened the database. Choose a new password: the old one will no longer open it.
